opus-5.5.text:
I should say up front that I'm not a film scholar. I'm a researcher who loves movies, and I watch them partly as a way to step outside my own field. But both directors have changed how I think about video.

With Bi Gan, the thing that really struck me is the long take. In *Kaili Blues*, and again in *Long Day's Journey into Night*, there's this continuous shot that goes on for close to an hour. The camera keeps moving through space, and time feels like it's folding in on itself: memory, dream and the present all blur together. As a computer vision person, I watched that and thought: this is what video actually is. It's not a stack of frames. It's a continuous experience of a world that persists even when the camera isn't looking at part of it.

A lot of our models still treat video as short clips, a few seconds and some frames we sample. Bi Gan's work reminded me that the interesting part of video is persistence, memory and the coherence of a space over a long time. If a model can't keep track of a room after the camera turns away and comes back, it doesn't understand that room. That connects directly to what I care about now: spatial intelligence, world models, and whether a system builds an internal representation of the world rather than just predicting the next pixels.

Jia Zhangke is almost the opposite pole for me. His films feel close to documentary. *Still Life* and *Platform* capture ordinary people, ordinary places, and the slow, sometimes brutal passage of time in a changing China. There's a lot of patience in just observing. What I take from that is a lesson about data and grounding. The real world is messy, mundane and long-tailed. Most of life isn't dramatic, curated YouTube highlights. If we want models that understand the world, they have to learn from that unglamorous, everyday visual experience, the way a person or a child actually takes in the world.

So I'd put it this way. Bi Gan made me think about time, memory and continuity as the core of video. Jia Zhangke made me think about reality, meaning observation grounded in the actual world rather than a polished version of it. Both point to the same thing: video isn't just another modality to add on top of language models. It might be the closest thing we have to how intelligence actually experiences the world. Cinema has been exploring that question for a hundred years, and I think we in AI are only starting to ask it seriously.

r001.rationale: The response links Bi Gan’s long takes to video as a continuous experience of a world that persists beyond the camera’s current view, connecting the films to continuous visual experience.

r002.rationale: It discusses persistence, spatial coherence, and representations beyond pixel prediction, but does not state that video understanding includes inferring causal relationships beyond visible pixels.

r003.rationale: It mentions Jia Zhangke’s ordinary places and the passage of time, but does not convey that each point in a film’s linear timeline needs spatial context to unfold its temporal meaning.

r004.rationale: The response says video is more than a stack of frames and describes a world persisting when the camera is not looking, conveying information about the world beyond any individual frame.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've actually thought about quite a lot, because my background is in computer vision, and for a long time "video" in our field just meant a stack of images with a time axis bolted on. You take an image model, you add temporal convolutions or temporal attention, and you call it a video model. And I think that framing is, frankly, a little impoverished.

What directors like Bi Gan and Jia Zhangke made me realize is that time in cinema is not a dimension you sample. It's the substance. If you watch the long take at the end of Long Day's Journey Into Night, that hour-long single shot, the whole point is that nothing in it is separable. The camera moving through space, the characters drifting in and out, the way memory and the present fold into each other, none of that can be cut into frames and recovered. The meaning lives in the continuity, in duration itself. Bi Gan is almost explicitly asking you to experience time as a material, something closer to how we actually remember than how we record.

Jia Zhangke does something different but related. His films are about a world that's changing underneath people in slow, almost imperceptible ways. Still Life, Platform, Mountains May Depart. You watch a town disappear, a factory close, a relationship stretch across decades. He's interested in the long temporal structure of ordinary life, the stuff that doesn't register as an "event" at any single moment but is unmistakable over years. And he'll hold a shot on a landscape or a face for much longer than a conventional editor would allow, because he trusts that the viewer will accumulate something.

So when I bring that back to research, a few things shift. First, I stop thinking of video understanding as "action recognition," where you classify a three-second clip. That's really just a slightly harder image problem. The interesting problem is long-horizon structure: what persists, what changes, what the world looks like when you're not looking. That's also, not coincidentally, the question underneath world models and self-supervised learning from video. If a model can predict what remains stable in a scene across a long take, it has learned something about physics and objects and agency that no caption would give it.

Second, these filmmakers make me suspicious of our benchmarks. The datasets we build tend to favor dense, legible motion, because that's what's easy to annotate and easy for a model to exploit. But most of the visual world is more like a Jia Zhangke shot than an action movie trailer. Slow, ambiguous, redundant. If our models can only handle the trailer, we haven't really solved video.

And third, there's an aesthetic lesson that's also a methodological one. Both directors trust the raw signal. They don't over-cut, they don't explain. There's a kind of humility toward the image, letting it carry information you didn't pre-specify. I think that's exactly the mindset you need for representation learning: resist the temptation to hand-design what matters, let the data speak at the scale it actually operates on. In that sense I'd say they shaped not just how I think about video, but how I think about what we should be asking a model to learn from the world in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response describes Bi Gan’s long take as continuous duration that cannot be recovered by cutting it into frames, and connects that experience to how people remember.

r002.rationale: It says video can teach models about physics, objects, and agency, but does not state that human video understanding infers causal relationships beyond visible pixels.

r003.rationale: It discusses Jia Zhangke’s long temporal structures and changing worlds, but does not connect each point in the timeline to spatial context needed for its temporal meaning.

r004.rationale: It says meaning in a long take cannot be recovered from separate frames and emphasizes understanding what persists or changes across time, conveying information about the world beyond any one frame.

astra-6.text:
For me, they suggest two different ways of thinking about time. When I watch Bi Gan, I’m struck by how a continuous shot can move through something that feels like memory or a dream. The camera records a physical space, but the experience isn’t simply a sequence of events. That makes me ask: if a model can track objects and describe actions, has it actually understood the video? Or is it missing the relationships that give that passage of time meaning?

With Jia Zhangke, I think more about how an ordinary scene carries a much larger context. A person, a street, a building—what matters is also how their relationships change over time. Understanding the visible action is only one layer.

So I’d frame the influence as a shift in the question. Video isn’t just an image-recognition problem with more frames. It’s a problem of understanding change, perspective, and what connects one moment to another. Cinema makes the gap between describing what’s visible and understanding an experience very clear.

r001.rationale: It describes Bi Gan’s continuous shots as evoking memory or dreams, but does not connect them to the continuity of human visual experience.

r002.rationale: It says meaningful relationships go beyond tracking objects and actions, but does not state that video understanding requires inferring causal relationships beyond visible pixels.

r003.rationale: It links people, places, and changing relationships over time, but does not convey that spatial context at each point in a linear timeline unfolds temporal meaning.

r004.rationale: It says video understanding involves change and connections across moments, but does not state that video conveys a global state of the world beyond any individual frame.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the connection is that video is more than a sequence of images. It’s also about time, memory, and how we experience a world. I wouldn’t claim a direct line from either filmmaker to a particular research decision, but their films offer a useful way to think about what our models might be missing.

With Bi Gan, you can think about continuity that isn’t simply chronological: a scene can connect to another through a feeling, a memory, or a dream. That raises an interesting research question: is understanding video just tracking what happens next, or does it require understanding relationships across time that aren’t explicit?

Jia Zhangke brings out another dimension: how individual lives sit within a changing social environment. An action alone doesn’t tell you very much without its context. For video research, that suggests we need to go beyond recognizing objects and movements toward understanding situations and how they develop.

So I would frame cinema as a reminder to be careful about our definition of understanding. A model might describe every frame accurately and still miss what the film is saying.

r001.rationale: The response describes Bi Gan’s continuity through feeling, memory, or dreams, but does not connect his long takes to the continuous nature of human visual experience.

r002.rationale: It raises the possibility of relationships across time that are not explicit, but does not clearly state that people infer causal relationships beyond visible pixels.

r003.rationale: It says individual actions need context within a changing social environment, but does not convey that each point on a linear timeline needs spatial context to unfold its temporal meaning.

r004.rationale: It says a model can describe every frame yet miss what a film is saying, but does not clearly state that video conveys a global state of the world beyond what any individual frame encodes.
